how-much-to-charge-for-a-gravel-driveway.text:
← Gravel driveway bid calculator

How much to charge for a gravel driveway

Excavation shops get shopped on a published $4 a square foot installed or $45 a ton dumped Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the depth or the dirt. Six hundred square feet of 4-inch crusher-run on ready grade you pick up at the quarry is a different job from eleven hundred square feet of 8-inch recycled stone that needs the existing surface excavated, hauled off, fabric, leftover truck tons, and a street apron.

Open the free gravel driveway bid calculator

Price trucks and compacted depth, not square feet

Quarries sell stone by the ton and often by the load. Convert length times width times finished compacted depth into loose cubic yards, add a compaction allowance (commonly 20 to 30 percent — the stone settles), then multiply by the stone’s tons per yard. You do not buy 1.1 truckloads. You buy two. Leftover tons on the last truck are paid for even if they are not spread. That leftover is how a “600 foot” special quietly becomes a 16-ton invoice.

The dirt is usually the job

Ready grade is a site walk. Grade-and-compact is a crew morning. Excavate-and-haul is dump tickets plus roughly twice the dirt hours of a grade. Matching a ready-grade 4-inch special on an 8-inch excavate-and-haul drive is how a sold job becomes a two-day loss after the first dump ticket.

Crusher-run, clean stone, recycled, and pea gravel are not the same install

Crusher-run (dense grade) locks together and spreads faster. Clean #57 drains and migrates more. Recycled crushed concrete is often the cheapest quarry invoice. Pea gravel looks finished and lays slower because it will not lock. The calculator prices the same drive four ways so you can see which stone still keeps the margin when the homeowner asks you to “just match the other guy.”

Fabric, apron, culvert, and slope

Quarry pickup is your truck. Quarry delivery is a load — leftover tons still need the truck. Geotextile fabric is square yards with overlap. A street apron and a culvert are their own tickets. Slope slows grade and spread, not the drive over.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the gravel driveway bid calculator. It is not a civil specification, a drainage design, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge for a gravel driveway?

Charge from compacted depth converted to tons, plus whole truckloads, soil prep, fabric, and a street apron — not a published per-square-foot special. A 600 sq ft 4-inch crusher-run pickup on ready grade is a different job from 1,120 sq ft of 8-inch recycled stone that needs the existing surface excavated and hauled off.

How many tons of gravel do I need for a driveway?

Convert length times width times compacted depth into loose cubic yards, add a compaction allowance (often 20 to 30 percent), then multiply by the stone's tons per yard (about 1.35 to 1.5). Quarries that sell by the load round up to a whole truck. Leftover tons on the last truck are paid for even if they are not spread.

Why is crusher-run cheaper to install than pea gravel?

Crusher-run locks together and spreads faster. Pea gravel costs more per ton at the quarry, migrates, and lays slower. Recycled crushed concrete is often the cheapest stone invoice but still needs the same dirt work as virgin stone.

Does soil prep change a gravel driveway bid?

Yes. Ready grade is a site walk. Grade-and-compact is a crew morning. Excavate-and-haul adds dump tickets and roughly twice the dirt hours of a grade. Those hours do not live in a per-foot special.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting hours and quarry rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own crews and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    Why does my tonnage never match the customer’s “length × width × depth” math?

    Because loose stone settles, and a quarry sells weight, not volume. This page does the three steps a square-footage number skips: it works out loose cubic yards from the pad, adds compaction on top (25% on the crusher-run preset — stone you pay for and then compact away), converts to tons using the stone’s own density, and only then prices it. Crusher run runs about 1.5 tons a cubic yard, clean #57 and recycled about 1.4, pea gravel about 1.35, so the same pad in two different stones is two different tonnages before a single price differs.

    Why does the price jump when I add a few feet of driveway?

    Trucks. Delivered stone is sold by the load, so tonnage rounds up to whole 16-ton trucks and the leftover tons on the last one are still on your invoice. Crossing from three loads to four adds a $145 truck trip and 0.6 hours whether you needed one ton more or fifteen. That step is the single most common reason a driveway bid built from a smooth per-foot rate loses money on a job only slightly bigger than the last one. Quarry pickup in your own truck has no per-load charge — that time is already in the trip hours.

    What does the stone choice actually change?

    Price per ton, how fast it spreads, and how much of it you need. Recycled crushed concrete starts cheapest at $22 a ton, crusher run $28, clean #57 stone $36, pea gravel $42. Spread rate moves the other way: crusher run covers about 400 sq ft an hour, recycled 380, clean stone 350, and pea gravel only 280 because it will not lock up and has to be worked. Switching stone refills those starting rates and leaves the wages and margin you typed alone.

    Why is “prep” a bigger line than I expect?

    Because it is the part the cheap special assumes away. A ready grade is zero dirt-work hours — the assumption behind every per-foot price you are being compared to. Machine grade and compact adds roughly one hour per 800 sq ft. Excavating the existing surface and hauling it off is double that, one hour per 400 sq ft, plus two $95 dump tickets by default. On a real driveway that is often the difference between the brochure number and the bid.

    Do I need fabric, an apron, or a culvert?

    They are separate ticks because they depend on the site, not the size. Geotextile fabric is priced by the square yard with an overlap allowance on top (10%, or 12% under pea gravel) and is what stops a soft subgrade eating the stone you just placed. A street apron starts at 2.5 hours and $420, a culvert at 3 hours and $380. None of them scale with the driveway, which is why folding them into a per-foot rate misprices both the small job and the large one.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser. Your bid is saved in this browser’s local storage so it is still here next visit, and a bid link you copy carries those same numbers in the page’s address rather than sending anything to a server. The optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your dimensions, wages, or prices.

    What’s the difference between the bid price and the walk-away price?

    The bid price already carries your target margin on top of labor, stone, trucking, and overhead. The walk-away price is the total cost underneath it — crew hours, ordered tons, truck loads, fabric, dump tickets, apron and culvert, travel and equipment — the point below which the driveway stops being profitable at all. Typing a number into “Price you’re considering” shows you the margin, or the loss, before you send it.

vs-a-flat-4-per-square-foot-special.html.text:
← Gravel Driveway Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $4-a-square-foot special

Gravel driveway shops are shopped by a published “$4 a square foot installed” special. That rate is priced for the easy job — ready grade, quarry pickup, no extras — and it cannot see excavation, haul-off, fabric, an apron, or a culvert, so a smaller job that needs all five can take more than three times the labor of a bigger job that needs none of them.

What a flat $4-a-square-foot special is

A flat per-square-foot number is the fastest thing a company can put on a postcard or a Facebook ad: one rate, times the drive's plan area, read back as a total. It is also the unit homeowners already compare between competing bids.

The rate was set for one job — commonly a ready-grade drive with no dirt work, picked up at the quarry rather than delivered, no fabric, no apron, and no culvert — and then quoted to the next caller, whether or not that driveway shares any of those.

What this calculator does instead

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the stone, drive length and width, compacted depth, compaction allowance, soil prep, delivery, fabric, apron, and culvert, plus your own wage, payroll burden, quarry and trucking rates, overhead, and target margin. It prices the trucks, the dirt work, and every extra as their own hours and cost lines — for this driveway, not a rate carried over from the last one.

What a flat per-square-foot special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same rate for a ready-grade drive and one that needs the existing surface excavated and hauled off, even though excavate-and-haul is double the grading hours plus two dump tickets. Prices grading hours from the prep method, so an excavate-and-haul job costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for delivery — quarry pickup and a delivered load sold by the ton get the same rate. Prices whole truckloads and the leftover tons on the last one separately from a pickup job's trip hours.
Has no line for fabric, an apron, a culvert, or a sloped site at all. Prices each of those as its own hours and material, on top of the base drive.
Bills stone choice inside the same blended per-square-foot number, if at all. Prices crusher-run, clean stone, recycled concrete, and pea gravel's own ton price and spread rate separately.
Gives the crew a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per square foot and the walk-away price alongside the total, so a shopped rate can be scored against real cost before you match it.

Same trade, two different jobs

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs — $24 hourly wage, 28% burden, $55 travel and equipment, 15% overhead, 20% target margin:

A 600 sq ft drive on ready grade, in crusher-run picked up at the quarry, with no fabric, apron, or culvert — the job a $4-a-square-foot special is usually built around — takes 3.2 crew-hours and this calculator prices it at $779.40 for the job — $1.30 per square foot, a fraction of the $4 headline rate.

A 400 sq ft drive — two-thirds the area — that needs the existing surface excavated and hauled off, delivered recycled stone, a sloped site, fabric, an apron, and a culvert takes 11.2 crew-hours, costs $2,788.78 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $3,485.97 — $8.71 per square foot. Quoting that job at the flat $4-a-square-foot rate reproduces $1,600.00 for the job, which is $1,188.78 below the job's own break-even cost — before counting the $1,885.97 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 20% target margin. A smaller drive, more than three times the labor, and a rate that looked generous on the easy job loses money the moment the excavator shows up.

Common questions

Why does a flat $4 a square foot special get a gravel driveway bid wrong?

Because plan area only measures the pad's footprint, not what it takes to build it. A 600 sq ft ready-grade drive picked up at the quarry and spread with no extras takes about 3.2 crew-hours on this calculator's own preset. A 400 sq ft drive that needs the existing surface excavated and hauled off, delivered recycled stone, a sloped site, fabric, an apron, and a culvert takes about 11.2 crew-hours -- more than three times the labor on two-thirds the area -- because excavation, haul-off, fabric, and site extras never show up in a per-square-foot number.

What job is the $4-a-square-foot number actually built around?

One specific job, usually the easiest one a company is willing to advertise: a ready-grade drive with no dirt work, picked up at the quarry rather than delivered, no fabric, no apron, and no culvert. It is a marketing price meant to get the phone to ring, not a number derived from any particular driveway's prep, stone, or site work.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

Using this calculator's own shipped cost inputs: the 600 sq ft ready-grade pickup job takes 3.2 crew-hours and prices at $779.40 for the job -- $1.30 per square foot, a fraction of the $4 headline rate. The 400 sq ft excavate-and-haul job with delivered recycled stone, a sloped site, fabric, an apron, and a culvert takes 11.2 crew-hours, costs $2,788.78 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $3,485.97 -- $8.71 per square foot. Quoting that job at the flat $4-a-square-foot rate reproduces $1,600.00 for the job, which is $1,188.78 below the job's own break-even cost -- before counting the $1,885.97 it falls short of this calculator's price at a 20% target margin.

Is a flat per-square-foot special ever a reasonable shorthand?

For a narrow band of jobs close to the one the special was priced on -- ready grade, quarry pickup, no fabric, no apron, no culvert -- a per-square-foot number can land close, or even leave a fat margin. The risk is quoting an excavate-and-haul job, delivered stone, a sloped site, or fabric and site extras the same way sight unseen, because the rate does not know the prep, the stone, or the site until the crew shows up, and by then the per-square-foot number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or material costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your quarry's stone, fabric, or trucking rates. It takes the stone, drive size, compacted depth, soil prep, delivery, fabric, apron, and culvert you enter, plus your own wage, payroll burden, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into crew-hours and a price for this job -- the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot special skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat per-square-foot special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest way to advertise that works until the driveway stops matching the one the special was priced on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it. The $779.40, $1.30, $2,788.78, and $3,485.97 figures above are this calculator's own arithmetic on its own shipped defaults (open the calculator and enter the same drive to reproduce them), not a claim about any specific contractor's real costs or any specific company's advertised price.

vs-jobber.html.text:
← Gravel Driveway Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is an account-based platform for running a home service company's whole operation, including scheduling the crew and invoicing the customer once a job is priced. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this gravel driveway job cost, before you offer it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is a field service management platform used by home service businesses — landscaping, excavation, cleaning, HVAC and general contracting among them — to run client management and online quoting, scheduling and crew dispatch, invoicing and online payments, and a client-facing hub, tied to one account used on an ongoing basis across every job the company runs. Jobber's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page. Public descriptions of that kind of field service software describe scheduling, invoicing and collecting payment for a job once its scope and price already exist; none describe working out what a gravel driveway job should cost from stone type, drive size, compacted depth, truckloads, soil prep and fabric before you quote it — which is the one thing this calculator does.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage a client list, dispatch a crew across a season, or collect a payment. It takes a driveway's stone choice — crusher-run, clean stone, recycled concrete, or pea gravel — drive length and width, compacted depth, truckloads, soil prep, fabric and apron, plus loaded crew wage, overhead and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price, the dirt-work share of the job, the leftover tons and the price per square foot — plus, if you already have a number on the table, a check of whether it clears your own break-even floor, and a printable customer proposal. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

Should I use this calculator or Jobber?

They do different jobs, and an excavation or landscape shop of any size will likely end up touching both.
